defect.evidence_quote: Whether police may, without a warrant, search the digital contents of a cell phone seized from an individual incident to arrest. ## Rule A warrant is generally required.
defect.locator_note: Black-letter callout ^rule-common-law-origins citing Boyd 624-30 and Riley 403.
defect.problem: The black-letter proposition is broader than the disclosed support verifies. Boyd partially supports the Entick/founding-history point, but the disclosed Riley pin-403 excerpt does not support the general-warrant/writs-of-assistance history or a second affirmative approval; no full opinion text is present.
defect.proposed_fix: Demote or narrow the rule to the Boyd-supported Entick historical-foundation proposition, and do not label it black-letter unless a verified second authority/pinpoint supports the general-warrant and writs-of-assistance formulation.

reasons: Boyd's disclosed pinpoints support only a narrower Entick/founding-history proposition, including that Entick states a foundational principle and that those propositions were in the minds of the framers.

Riley pin-403 in the lake concerns cell-phone searches incident to arrest and a general warrant requirement; it does not mention general warrants, writs of assistance, Entick, or founding-generation history.
Because the callout is framed as black-letter, it needs at least two affirmative approvals; the disclosed evidence supplies at most one partial approval.
residual_risks: The Boyd and Riley pinpoints are marked quote_fidelity mismatch/slip-only, and no text/*.txt opinion files are available for verbatim or holding checks.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Limit the statement to: Boyd treats Entick as a historical foundation for the Fourth Amendment, unless a verified Riley history passage is added.
